For the auto reversing and gear shift, I’d say I rely on that 9 time out of 10. Paul obviously wasn’t familiar with it, but the Tesla doesn’t just change gears willy nilly on you.  It’s smarter than that, and is expecting certain conditions. For example, you hardly want your car by default automatically engaging reverse whenever you approach a barrier, otherwise it will go into reverse each time you park. However it will detect things like a three point turn quiet well, or if your parallel parking, it works well to detect that you’ve pulled in and backed up to the car behind you, and sensibly changes gears after you push the brake to finish the manoeuvre , while telling you what it’s about to do. 

The system works remarkably well (not perfectly), I think Paul just needs to be familiar with it.

comment:
Electric Vehicles, or EVs, Are Not Cars

The government and auto industry wants us to believe that EVs are interchangeable with gas-powered vehicles.

EVs are not a “car” as we know them. EVs are experimental transportation devices that the government wants us to accept as a car replacement.

I believe the rollout of them was extremely premature. They look like cars, and seem to function like cars, but they are not cars.

Words and their traditional definitions matter.

Using the word car for an EV is misleading. I try to avoid it.

EVs are a completely different machine and when purchasing one that should be our mindset.

Replacements For Vital Machines (Evs For Cars) Must Outperform Their Predecessors To Be Universally Adopted

For a new product or invention, which an EV is, to replace a tried and true significant part of our daily lives, like our cars, it has to be a better choice.

Do EVs outperform cars in all important areas?
How should a car replacement be better?
1) Cheaper purchase price, lifetime maintenance and disposal.
2) Better performance, road handling and driving range.
3) As many or more locations to “refuel” and lower recharging times than refueling. Overall more convenient and time saving than gas powered vehicles.
4) Safer in all ways, including charging away from home.
5) Seamless and transparent replacement for our current experience with cars.
6) EVs should be less expensive to insure.
7) End of Life Disposal must be cheaper and more environmentally friendly.


How do EVs stack up in those five categories?
1) EVs are more expensive than gas-powered vehicles. Overall costs over time are much higher for EVs. Even if they were cheaper, the current negative impacts of the loss of convenience and functionality make EVs not worth replacing our cars with experimental replacements. Government subsidies paid to corporations and individuals approach $50,000 per EV. An EV is less functional, yet more expensive? Who thought of this great system?
2) EVs have much higher average horsepower, but other than that the driving experience is not much different and is sometimes deficient. Range anxiety is real and total miles available on a full charge falls terribly behind a full tank of gas.
3) Gas stations are much safer and more convenient than EV charging stations. On the road charging can average ten times longer than refueling with gasoline. EVs fail miserably here.
4) The level of danger using an unmanned EV charging station at night in a deserted parking lot is not tenable, compared to gas stations which have personnel, lights and security cameras. EV battery explosions are commonplace.
5) EVs are not a cheaper, more functional replacement for our cars.
6) A true car replacement would be cheaper to insure. Middle class families already can’t afford car insurance.
7) EV End of Life Disposal? Is there even a plan? What is the tested process for dismantling and disposing of the dead batteries? I am sure this will be very costly for the unfortunate consumer who is the last owner.

EVs fail on almost every measure.

This certainly does not make a great case for EVs.

Using EVs dramatically changes your entire driving experience, one of the most important parts of our daily lives.

There are so many unanswered questions about the impact on us if the government were to ban gas-powered vehicles in favor of EVs.

Mandating EVs will change our way of life.

As with other government experiments in the recent past, they want us to be the test subjects.

I propose we opt out of this government experiment and all others in the future.

Fad For Wealthier People

EVs are still a fad for wealthier people for the most part. Currently they are mostly an option for owners of free standing single family homes and less often owners of townhouses with a garage.

And even for those free standing single family homeowners, once you have more than one EV, it can quickly become impractical, cumbersome and unworkable.

There are government laws forcing apartment complex owners and townhouse communities to allow residents to install charging stations, but they are not widely used.

The vast majority of renters and townhouse owners don’t have the ability to purchase an EV as they can’t charge them nightly.

EVs require access to a power supply that can extend to your EV where they are parked overnight. While away from home needing a charge, you need to find a charging station.

For people who own free standing homes, with a traditional garage and driveway setup, this is relatively simple and most practical. But even then, a family with two or more EVs may not be able to charge all of them overnight. Once you expand beyond one EV, things begin to fall apart.

Many townhouse owners are in the same predicament as apartment renters.
Renters of any type of home usually don’t have the ability or finances to install the systems needed to charge an EV. They would also need permission from the landlord.

Even if an apartment complex or townhouse association installed a few, having this done on mass scale for all apartment and townhouse residents is not practical for decades to come, if at all.

Townhouses, although purchased as a residence, are more likely to be a temporary stop to a free standing home, and so installing a charging station may not be worth the investment.

Excluding these drivers will stall or make impossible the complete replacement of gas-powered vehicles with EVs. 

So, what percentage of drivers are in free standing single family homes? This is the true market for EVs on the consumer level. And, again, only for one EV in the family.

Let’s take a look at the figures below.

It will tell us what % of us have severe barriers to entering the EV space.

132,000,000 (A) - USA Households			            	
83,000,000 (B) - Detached single family homes						
49,000,000 (C=A -B) - USA Households With Barriers To Entry Into EV Space	                
37.12% (D=C/A) - % USA Households With Barriers To Entry Into EV Space
233,000,000 (E) - Drivers In The USA			
86,000,000	(D×E) - USA Drivers With Barriers To Entry Into EV Space			

86,000,000 out of 233,000,000 U.S. drivers cannot practically transition to EV use. 

This 37% of drivers who cannot use an EV is important to remember, as it impacts the rest of the problems EV owners face.

Safety Issues At Charging Stations On The Road

Again, remember, we are imagining a world where gasoline is no longer needed and so gas stations would become a novelty.

So, with only EVs in everyday use, there will be times we need to charge away from home. Where will this take place? There is some EV charging infrastructure built out, but there are many problems. And this is with a very small percentage of EVs on the road.

Imagine, again, that only EVs were allowed. The infrastructure needed is unfathomable.

And what is the infrastructure for remote charging going to look like?

I have serious concerns here as should you.

When we need gas, we simply find an open gas station.

Gas stations have security cameras and personnel when they are open.

We take these well lit locations with employees and security cameras for granted. These safety features do not exist at EV charging locations. Most will be in parking lots of retail shopping centers with no attendants.

This decreases security and increases waiting times.  That is what they are proposing. We should not accept these severe regressions of course. 

Parents, let me ask you. Would you accept your children going into dark and empty parking lots, when retail stores are closed, to charge up for 20 or 30 minutes by themselves with no personnel on site?

Of course you would not.

No security. No one in government is talking about this. Remember, they want to eliminate the safe gas stations that are an integral part of our culture and replace them with this.

This is just another barrier I don’t hear anyone discussing.

EVs are not interchangeable with gas-powered vehicles. They are a completely different machine. They are not cars.

Consumers need to demand the same level of security measures and functionality that gas stations provide.

Since this video talks about california, lets look at cali.  

at an average of 26-33 cents per kwh cost (assuming home only charging) every 60kwh costs about $16-20.  assuming 3.75whpm in the real world use (3.75 miles per kwh if im correct) would be 225 miles, some EVs are as low as 3.0 whpm which means your costs can be higher.  we will assume for this comparison, that the EV is operating in an optimal climate (not extreme cold) for these numbers.    
real california cost average is 33c per kwh.  so this estimate would actually be considered too low.
but for comparison, im using 60kwh vs a 10 gallon tank.    
a hybrid car that gets 45 miles per gallon, at $4.50 a gallon would cost $45 for 10 gallons, and 450 miles per 10 gallons. (the prius has a 10 gallon tank, and gets over 50mpg, but i lowballed it on purpose)
the EV would have to be charged 2x for the same/similar range, $36-40 on the low end estimate to go the same range.

a hybrid refuels in 5 minutes, an EV takes, at home, 6-30 hours (depending on charger type), and in public charging 25-40 minutes assuming its not full, or waiting time.  

now lets talk about public charger costs, which are higher than residential.  so those that use or need public charging, will cost 1.50-2x more than residential rates.  which means charging 60kwh to go 225 average miles will cost someone $30-$40, or $60-$80 compared to a 45mpg hybrid car costing $45-50 to refuel.  

then theres insurance, for some its 2x higher than a gas car.  

So where is the real benefit of EV compared to a better mpg hybrid in a place like california?  the costs to operate daily would run pretty similar, and give an owner far more freedom with a hybrid.   in cali, often the chargers are backed up too since they got so popular and i think potential owners are seeing this and backing off.  

Average range of 270 miles as you stated in the video for most EVs, is only in OPTIMAL climates (30F-95F).  we all know cold reduces 10-40% depending on how cold it is.  at 28F i lost less than 10%.  what they dont tell you is when its over 105F outside your range tanks as well, loss of 25-40% depending on habits and temps over 110F as over 110F it is even more reduced.  
California urban areas generally are within optimal climate or minimal outside of it, but traffic may reduce that range as well.

I have a Tesla  2023 Model 3 LR that has an EPA of 358 miles. After one year the battery degradation is 11 percent and I'm at  333 miles at 100% charge on 19" sport rims. The major point everyone is missing when they say there is plenty of range when your EPA rating is 300 miles at 100 charge, is the battery in the car is used when you run the heater/ac or charge other items like a cell phone. Also, if the road you are traveling on has some elevation or you need to keep up with the flow of traffic and go 70 to 75 mph from time to time on the freeway. All the aforementioned reduce the available energy in your EV battery which also affects your range. 

If the goal is for EV's to go mainstream and compete with ICE cars, the base battery range for EV's has to be 400 to 450 miles to a full charge so we can "really" use the car and not worry about silly things like how much we use the heater or ac! Or worry about going a little over the speed limit or choosing a tire rim size one size above the standard that is sold with the car.

For full EV adoption, you can't expect a common person to become a "scientist" when they just want to get into their car and take a simple road trip or go down the street to the grocery store. The car manufactures also must let third party repair shops work on the cars and the parts of EV's have to go down in price or  full EV adoption is not going not happen...period.

comment: These "extra" taxes for EV's can be expected. Given the federal gas tax of 18.4 cents/gal, and state gas taxes (as an example, in Maryland) of 47 cent/gal, and assuming a fleet average of 24.3 mpg, an ICE vehicle owner who drive 10,000 miles per year will be paying something on the order of $72 to the feds and $185 to the state in gas taxes. That's $250 or so per year in highway maintenance revenues that ICE vehicle owners are paying that EV owners are not. We should not be surprised that governments will be seeking a way to recoup those lost revenues. It feels like a "persecution" of EV's because ICE vehicle owners don't "feel" that $250 since those fees are "hidden" in the price per gallon of gas. A better approach would be to charge everyone, ICE & EV, an annual registration fee based on milage driven, and redirect gas taxes to environmental clean-up.

Some states in the USA allow vehicle monitors for insurance,  semis use monitors, and are taxed by the mile to use roads in each State. Monitor use in California is restricted without permission.

I see yearly reporting of miles or monitors coming to all vehicles in California based on type, weight, miles driven, and roads used. 
Why?
 
Within the State, roads are maintained by private parties, City, County, State, or Federal government. 
Currently, fuel taxes in the State flow to each of these government bodies based on the gallons of fuel purchased. 
To "fairly" tax different vehicle types (EVs, PHEVs, ICE) based on usage, yearly reporting or monitoring of miles driven will be necessary. 

Solar power and EVs are prevalent in the State of California.

I counted the number of cars entering a busy shopping mall by type for 30 minutes.

The Federal government required auto manufacturers to add the monitoring in 1994 and again in 1996 (OBDII information port). theres still reasons why a gas car just makes more sense, or a hybrid.  EVs cannot handle extreme temps.  hot, or cold.  this being the reason why 2/3 of the country do not want EV mandates, they cannot compete in many real world situations.

Im a mechanic. We don't see teslas often but occasionally people bring them in for tires or a state inspection. My first time driving one was a nightmare. There is literally no indication that the car is ready to be driven. You just have to know that once you sit down you can drive. Finding the info for the car such as the millage was obnoxious because you have to go through menus on the tablet thing. No one at the shop knew that if you leave the credit card thing in there that the car just stays on so we drained way more battery than needed which didn't make the customer very happy. Putting them on a lift is obnoxious. They have very specific lift points and you need to use these block things that only tesla sells. Luckily this first time the customer had some. And when I test drove it, it was not a good experience. That was a few years ago and I've driven a good amount of them now, including a cyber truck and I genuinely don't understand the appeal. They're not comfortable to sit in, they don't suck you into the seat when you let'er eat like a gas car, they don't feel good driving over bumps and pot holes. 

Also they may be fast for a grand total of about a fourth of a mile, but otherwise they are incredibly sluggish and boaty. I haven't had the opportunity to track one yet. However my friend who has done that drove nearly 5 seconds slower than in a base trim honda civic.

comment:
The best EV Nio!!! 
Base on fast charging car batteries just degrades the battery just like your mobile phone. Eventually the battery degrades so much, the car loses its value if you can’t swap out the battery. Replacing the batteries is tedious and expensive. Battery swapping centralizes battery management, so health is always maintained by the company, and in theory your EV could last forever.

Plus, you can always swap out different battery sizes. If you needed to make a 1000km journey, you could just swap out to a larger battery for a day or two, which is much more cost effective than buying a permanent 1000km range battery that you’ll only use once in a while (plus it degrades over time). Swapping also makes upgrades easy and feasible, like if they came up with a new version of a battery that was more efficient for example.

Swapping takes 3 mins, and is completely autonomous. You can drive up to a swap station, get out and get a coffee, it will park itself in the swapping bay, and by the time you get back with your coffee, you’ll be ready to go. For charging, you need to park, get out of the car, plug in the charger, and still wait at least another 20-30 mins and you still won’t have a full battery. Imagine on a crowded day where all chargers are used up, how long would you have to wait? This happens often in China during the Chinese new year. Autonomous swapping would also pave the way for a robo-taxi ecosystem where cars car drive itself, and swap out the batteries themselves. You can’t do that with charging (remember the awkward arm charger). 

NIO also comes with fast charging, not just battery swapping. So why would anyone not want 2 options (swapping and charging) over having only 1 (charging).

This is not even a question of what people want .... I would love to have a 100% electric vehicle.  Its about what is practical.  Currently available rechargeable battery technology is not sufficient for a fully electric vehicle that matches the usability of an internal combustion vehicle (ICE). Also the power grid and typical home wiring is also not ready for the massive charging current demands that widespread use of such vehicles would result in. comment: Good video and mainly informative with some interesting points, but i felt you were not grasping the 'whole EV experience'.  Is 6 months enough time to get into the mindset?  I have been driving EV's for well over 2 years and frankly loved every vehicle i have driven, and its been quite a few.  So, Kia EV6 lovely car, Hyundai Ioniq 5, still a stunning design and so spacious inside, Polestar 2, odd seating with a large centre console that makes the driving position cramped, VW ID.3 & 4 simply stunning and the Cupra Born (basically an ID.3 but takes the looks and design to the next step).  Mercedes EQA, B and C are again lovely but lack in range somewhat and then the BMW iX40 - stunning to look at and a music sound system to die for, but on the 40 sadly lacking range.  Each EV stands alone with quirks, but they all rely on a charging infrastructure which is sadly lacking in some areas such as Wales, or to be more precise Mid-Wales.  My favourite car is a toss up between the Tesla Model 3 Long Range AWD and the BMW iX40 Xdrive, as they both have their strengths.  Both are very minimalistic when it comes to actual controls and buttons, but for sheer comfort the BMW iX wins hands down but for range the Tesla Model 3 LR, plus the Tesla Supercharger network is fantastic and so much cheaper per kW that any i have used and they seem to be expanding many sites and increasing numbers.  I was in Rugby Moto services around 8 months ago where there were 12x Gridserve 350kWh chargers and 12x Tesla Superchargers - last week running that way again, there are now 28x Tesla Chargers.  Safe driving everyone

comment:
If you are basing buying this car solely on track performance, then your a moron. They completely missed the fact that it scored over 300 miles on Edmunds real world range tests. You can commute and still out accelerate and/or pass when needed, most of the cars on the road in most situations. Unless you live in some very low traffic rural area with insanely well kept roads, you are not going to get into some type or epic racing battle. Which is also insanely dangerous. You should never buy any stock car and expect it to be safe on a race track. That is what race cars are for. And if it matters so much to you, then actually build a track car. If you are really stuck on a daily driver being your track car, put a suspension and brakes on it. It will still be much easier and more cost effective than trying to put 510Hp in another under powered EV. Watching this review was like watching stupid CPU reviews where they complain the new CPU only does 280 vs 320 FPS. No one is gaming at 280, and even 500 is not going to make you better. Just like having some stupid capable track car is not going to make you a better driver. Especially on the road in real world conditions. Most of the idiots you see who crash their sports cars on the road do so because the suspension is too stiff. In any weather/road condition where is is not dry and flat, a softer suspension is better for safety. It is more forgiving and will not get you into one of those unrecoverable slides and/or spins that you see in 90% of the crash videos.

And don't get me started on the driving skill, or lack there of shown in this video. Anyone who has raced and actually tried to get good track times with a car that is lacking in an area, uses where it is not lacking to make up for it as much as possible. That is basically what racing is all about. Race car drivers don't just keep abusing the weakness of their car and then cry about it. Drivers that actually win use the strengths of the car and minimize the weaknesses to achieve better performance. The simplest thing that could have been done, is to use the HP to accelerate faster and not carry such a high top speed in the straights into the corners. If you accelerate up to a speed faster than the last model and keep at that speed, breaking into the turn at the same speed is no different than the last vehicle. By not over driving it, and with more acceleration, it should have easily been able to do all the laps with much better times than the previous model. It would have been logical to to let the car cool off, learn to drive it a little, and run the laps again. Getting out and throwing a tantrum because it did not drive like a full on track car just because it has performance in the name and a track button on the screen is being a little baby. In generations before us, men have adapted and overcome problems. That is how we got where we are today. Any car is terrible with a bad driver.

Hagerty has done an absolutely mindblowingly good comparison of the 2024 Tesla Model 3P with the BMW M3 Competition.  Both cars being strictly factory conform (including tires).

Hagerty positively loved the behavior of the model 3P on the track, and even ranked it first on drifting behavior. On a single best lap, the BMW beat the Tesla by a good second, but it was entirely due to it having tires better suited for the track.  They even did a 15 straight lap comparison.  Yes, the BMW did a bit better on that test... but the Tesla' brakes did NOT overheat.  How can those two reviews come with so different results on the topic of track behavior?  Having said this, how many potential customers will ever take their car to a track? 1%? 2%?

comment:
great video, but regarding your remark about how "most EVs tend to run out of steam at higher speeds", that's not really a problem with EVs, it's a problem with their transmission. Most manufacturers don't bother putting multi-speed transmissions on EVs because profit-wise it's not worth it, so they usually just put a single short final drive ratio. This means that the car maxes out the motor's rpm way too soon, and is only limited by motor spin speed rather than power. Given them another gear or a longer final drive ratio and they'll easily get higher top speed. If you aren't convinced, just look at how high the top speeds of EV bullet trains are compared to steam or even diesel-electric locomotives. Electric is literally meant for top speed.

Edit: forgot to mention that current EV cars are only using permanent magnet DC motors rather than the AC motors on bullet trains. AC motors have constant torque so the hp just keeps increasing as the rpm increases and can reach some extreme numbers

comment:
I have a few really big issues that looks to be unresolved in FSD 12.5.6 still. 
-FSD still largely ignores the road surface, including potholes, some/many speedbumps, and likely all kinds of snow and black ice. 98% of FSD videos are in ideal driving conditions. There are no current videos in bad weather or slippery roads.
-Still not convinced about the cameras working for FSD in (heavier?)rain and there are very few FSD videos in rain.
-There appears to still be short-term desicion making for lane choices, which will be a really hot topic in rush hour traffic. If your car wants to change lane late after driving past a long queue in another lane, the best outcome is other drivers becoming angry (at me and in the long term Teslas) but could also result in being blocked or worse. Not sure what queue etiquette is in the US and other countries though.
-Front first perpendicular parking would also be great so I can access the trunk.

comment:
As a current model 3 owner I think improving the suspension is a great step forward. The current suspension is great in that the car does not roll into corners, however, with tyres at their pressure rating the ride is harsh (reduce tyre pressure a little to improve).  The suspension also can thump a bit if it hits a bump in the road. However, having said that, overall it is a great car to drive with responsive steering and amazing acceleration. 
The bad things are no foot room in the back seat, dumb external door handles, seats that while reasonable are not as comfortable as a BMW 3 series seat, bad positioning of window controls on the driver side door causing accidental opening of rear window, cheap carpet material, not enough sound deadening for road noise, should have a HUD for speed and status info, and the multi functionality of the right hand stalk can be a problem (if you have just been driving a vehicle with the turn indicator on the right and want to turn left in the Tesla accidentally pushing the right stalk up at low speed it will put you in reverse, which is not such a good idea).   Oh and while I am at it the whole way the door opens with a push button, but still has an emergency release handle seems pointless and should be redesigned.
The there is autopilot, which although a great benefit a lot of the time has serious limitations. This is not FSD but as a taste of FSD it does not inspire confidence.  I won’t go through all the issues here, but based on my own experience driving an Australian version it can cause accidents with a tendency to jam on the brakes too soon and too often.
I would agree with the comments made about the updated model 3. Removing the stalks is just silly.  Using the screen to select forward and reverse is dumb. If the screen fails the vehicle is dead in the water, you need to be outside aware when setting the vehicle in motion, not trying to focus on a screen and hitting/sliding your finger over it.  More premium seats would be really good and get rid of the silly external door handles
